title: Part Finder
context: Grade 5, the pages on a per cent of a quantity. An adult sees multiplying by a fraction. What the pages are doing is taking a part of a whole: fifty per cent means half, ten per cent a tenth, and any per cent is that many hundredths of the quantity. A measure is written in the unit the answer asks for first, and a question about what is left needs the part used taken away.

writeup.why: Find a per cent of a number from a benchmark, from lots of 10% or as the per cent over 100 times the number, find a per cent of a measure in the unit asked for, and find what is left after a per cent is used.
writeup.look: A whole bar labelled 100% across the working area, with the Fold and Cut into ten buttons over it. The fraction line lies under the bar, and the Unit fact card and the Use button join on the later phases.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Part Finder' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the per cent of the bar that is lit. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The whole bar lies at x 110, y 300, 900 long and 90 tall, labelled Whole and 100% at its right end, the quantity written on it in deep blue. The Fold buttons, Half, Quarter and Tenth, the Double button and the Cut into ten button sit in a row above it at y 220, each labelled in words. Folds and cuts draw near-black lines across the bar, every part exactly one width, each labelled with its share. Parts lit by dragging turn amber and are counted in lots of ten per cent in the running count. The fraction line lies under the bar at x 110, y 430, working the per cent over one hundred times the quantity step by step; when Double lays a second whole bar of the same length under the first, the fraction line drops to y 520. The Unit fact card stands at x 110, y 560, its fact in violet. On the fourth phase the Use button stands at x 700, y 560, the used part lifts off the bar in rose, labelled Used, down to y 640, and the part that stays is green, labelled Left. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a % key and unit keys for g, kg, mL, litres, cm, m and km. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. The part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, labelled Given. The per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, and what is left after a part is used, is green, labelled Answer or Left. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion, labelled Both terms or Times 100. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet, labelled Unit fact. The part used, taken away or not won is rose, labelled Used or Not won. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey, labelled Place holder, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the % sign is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The bar shows the last quantity with its part lit, the unit fact that was used, and the part left in green.

writeup.delight: On the fourth phase, when Use is tapped, the rose part lifts gently off the bar and floats down, and the green part left behind glows once with its label Left.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing lit. On the first phase the whole bar holds a number and the Fold buttons wait over it. On the second the bar holds a number with the Cut into ten button lit. On the third it holds a measure in one unit, and the question card asks for another unit. On the fourth it holds a measure of something to be used, with the Use button waiting. One thing moves, once: the first button the phase needs gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: A quantity of the child's own, folded, cut into tenths, rewritten in another unit, or used and left. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on benchmark per cents, a per cent of a number, a per cent of a measure, and what is left.

observations.soWhat: the benchmark per cents are a half, a quarter, a tenth and double.

observations.why: ten equal parts of a whole are tenths, and a tenth is ten hundredths.
observations.soWhat: a per cent that is a count of tens is found from ten per cent first.

source_tool.description: A whole bar 900 long lies across the working area, labelled Whole and 100% at its right end, with the quantity the question gives written on it in deep blue. A row of Fold buttons, Half, Quarter and Tenth, folds the bar into two, four or ten equal parts and names each part's per cent, and a Double button lays a second whole bar beside the first. A Cut into ten button splits the bar into ten equal parts, each labelled with its share of the quantity, and dragging across parts lights them amber and counts them in lots of 10%. A fraction line under the bar writes the per cent over 100 times the quantity, and works it out step by step. A Unit fact card, chosen from a short list, rewrites a measure in violet before anything is worked: 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 litre = 1000 mL, 1 m = 100 cm or 1 km = 1000 m. On the last phase a Use button lifts the chosen part off the bar in rose, labelled Used, and the part that stays is green, labelled Left. A number pad types any quantity, per cent or answer. The running count at the top left of the canvas is the per cent of the bar that is lit.
source_tool.art_direction: Paper strips and a measuring jug / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: hundred grids of ten rows and ten columns, strips cut into equal cells, fraction bars with their denominator of one hundred built beside them, measuring jugs, tapes and scales with their units written on them.

Every whole is drawn the same size as every other whole it is compared with, and its parts are exactly equal: a strip of ten has ten cells of one width, and a hundred grid is always a full ten by ten.
A whole is always labelled 100%, so the child sees what one hundred per cent means before any part is named.
Where shaded cells are counted, exactly the stated number is shaded, and they stay countable at a glance: full columns of ten first, then single cells.
A product that becomes a per cent is always written with its brackets, and the % sign comes last. A decimal reaches a per cent through its hundredths, never by moving anything.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: cells filling a grid, both terms of a fraction growing together, a unit fact rewriting an amount, or a used part lifting away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a cell or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a per cent plays in a piece of working: the part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, and the per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, with what is left after a part is used, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet. The part used, taken away or not won is rose. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its outline, and the % sign itself is near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Both terms, Unit fact, Used, Not won, Left and Place holder, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Fold the bar again, or find ten per cent first.
voice.onNext: A new amount. Which part does the question want?
voice.opening: A whole bar, ready to be folded or cut.
voice.onFinish: You found every part, and said which part was asked for.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Fold, cut, change units and use parts as you like.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After the class has folded paper strips into halves, quarters and tenths and poured water from a measuring jug. The tool is what cuts any quantity into ten equal parts and lifts the used part away, which paper can only draw once.

answer_key.rule: A per cent of a number is that many hundredths of it. 50% is half, 25% is a quarter, 10% is a tenth and 200% is double. A per cent that is a count of tens is found from 10% first: 30% is three lots of 10%. Any per cent can also be found as the fraction over 100 times the number. A measure is written in the unit the answer asks for first, and the unit fact is said: 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 litre = 1000 mL, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m. What is left is the whole take away the part used, or the per cent left of the whole. Say which amount the question asks for.
answer_key.wrong: The bar is shown again with the child's answer lit on it beside the right part, both measured against the same whole, so the two sizes are seen side by side, and the step where they part is lit amber. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A quarter of 44 is 44 shared into 4 equal parts: 11 in each part.
items.question: What is 25% of 44?
items.checkpoint: 50% is half, 25% is a quarter, 10% is a tenth and 200% is double.
items.misconception: Halving 44 only once and giving 22, which is half, not a quarter.

steps: Or find 10% first: 10% of 40 is 4, and 60% is six lots of it: 6 x 4 = 24.
items.question: What is 60% of 40?
items.checkpoint: A per cent of a number is that many hundredths of the number.
items.misconception: Finding 10% of 40 and stopping at 4, which is only one tenth of the number.

steps: First write the measure in the unit the answer asks for.
items.question: How many grams is 30% of 3 kg?
items.checkpoint: Write the measure in the unit the answer asks for, and say the unit fact.
items.misconception: Writing 0.9 g, which keeps the number found for kilograms but names it in grams.

steps: First find the part poured out: 40/100 x 1500 = 600, so 600 mL is poured out.
Then take it away: 1500 - 600 = 900, so 900 mL of juice is left.
Check another way: the part left is 60%, and 60% of 1500 mL is 900 mL.
items.question: A jug holds 1500 mL of juice, and 40% of it is poured out. How much juice is left in the jug?
items.checkpoint: Say which amount is asked: the part used or the part left.
items.misconception: Giving 600 mL, the part poured out, when the question asks what is left.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: If 45% of a garden has been dug, what per cent has not been dug?
How many centimetres is 20% of 3 m?
items.final_answer: 60 cm. 1 m = 100 cm, so 3 m = 300 cm, and 20% of 300 cm is 60 cm

items.question: A sack holds 5 kg of rice, and 20% of it is used. How many grams of rice are left?
A ribbon is 2 m long, and 45% of it is cut off. How many centimetres of ribbon are left?

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

teaching_notes: Fold paper strips into halves, quarters and tenths before the tool opens, and name each fold as a per cent: fifty per cent means half. Find ten per cent first when a per cent is a count of tens. Change a measure into the unit the answer asks for before finding the per cent, and say the unit fact aloud. Ask which amount a question wants, the part used or the part left, before anything is worked. Use counts and measures only: the exercise's own amounts are the child's to find.
generation_prompt: Build a per cent of a quantity tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A whole bar 900 long, labelled Whole and 100%, holds the quantity the question gives in deep blue. Fold buttons, Half, Quarter and Tenth, fold it into equal parts and name each part's per cent, and a Double button lays a second whole beside it. A Cut into ten button splits it into ten equal parts, each 10% of the whole, and dragging lights parts amber in lots of 10%. A fraction line under the bar writes the per cent over 100 times the quantity and works it out. A Unit fact card rewrites a measure in violet: 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 litre = 1000 mL, 1 m = 100 cm or 1 km = 1000 m. On the last phase a Use button lifts the chosen part off in rose, labelled Used, and the rest stays green, labelled Left. A number pad types quantities, per cents and answers.
